faqs.q: Coyotes are in our St. Petersburg neighborhood — will trapping help?
faqs.a: Rarely, and we will explain why rather than sell it. Urban coyote territories refill — remove one pair and the next disperses into the vacancy within weeks, while the attractants (outdoor pet food, unsecured trash, free-roaming cats) keep teaching them the route. What works is the city's playbook: cats indoors, dogs leashed, food secured, and confident hazing of bold animals. A coyote that is sick, injured, or genuinely dangerous is a call to the city and FWC. Our work is the raccoon in your attic; the coyote file belongs to coexistence, and honestly run, it works.

faqs.q: What should I do about armadillo digging in Largo?
faqs.a: Nine-banded armadillos dig for grubs and earthworms in lawns and flower beds, and they are common throughout most of Florida, including Largo. A live-trapped armadillo may be released on-site, or released within the same county on 40 or more contiguous acres with the landowner's written permission, within 24 hours — those are the Florida rules, and we follow them. We also talk through fencing and grub management, because trapping alone rarely ends digging in good habitat.

faqs.q: Something is living under our Largo manufactured home. What is the process?
faqs.a: First we identify it — skunk, opossum, armadillo, and raccoon all use the space under manufactured homes, and they are handled differently. Then the residents come out, and the real work starts: the skirting. Damaged or loose skirting is why the space was available, so we repair or replace the failed sections and back the vulnerable runs with buried wire so the next animal that tests the perimeter meets a wall. Skirting patched at one hole fails at the next weakest panel, which is why we assess the whole perimeter rather than the entry of the week.

faqs.q: Why do roof rats keep coming back to our street in Largo?
faqs.a: Because the street itself is their habitat — palms, citrus, and canopy oaks connected by fences and wires, with a roof every fifty feet. A single house can absolutely be solved: seal its roofline in metal, cut the branch and palm bridges, and trap out the residents, and that house stays rat-free. What no one can honestly sell you is a rat-free street. We will show you the bridges and entries on your home specifically, so your money goes to the part of the system with your name on it.

Largo.wildlife_intro:
In Largo, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — Florida's most densely populated county — continuous coastal suburbs and barrier-island beaches — and features such as Tampa Bay shoreline, Boca Ciega Bay, Lake Tarpon, Weedon Island Preserve keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Largo jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

Largo is the dense middle of Florida's most crowded county, and its wildlife work is urban density work. Mid-century suburbs, mobile and manufactured home communities, and commercial corridors stand wall to wall from the bay to the beaches, and the animals have organised themselves accordingly: roof rats running the palms and the fence lines, raccoons in the attics of the ranch homes and the voids of the older commercial buildings, opossums under every low deck, and armadillos in whatever soft ground the county has left unpaved. In Largo the habitat is the neighbourhood itself — the canopy, the drainage easements, and the other houses.

Largo Lake and the drainage corridors that cross the city give the population its highways, and the sheer number of roofs means exclusion here is a street-level game: a raccoon sealed out of one attic on a dense block tests the next four houses the same week. Our Largo inspections assume the neighbours' problems and yours are related, and the sealing we spec is built for an animal that lives thirty feet away, not one passing through. The manufactured-home communities add their own specialty — skirting. Every gap in a home's skirting is a door at ground level, and Largo's skunks, opossums, and armadillos all know it.
Largo.extendedBody:
Manufactured homes and the skirting problem

Largo's manufactured and mobile home communities are some of the most wildlife-pressed housing in Pinellas County, for one structural reason: the space beneath the home. A manufactured home sits over a crawl void enclosed only by skirting, and damaged, loose, or poorly fitted skirting is an open door to skunks, opossums, armadillos, and raccoons — which then live directly under the floor, and the homeowner hears and smells everything. The fix is specific: remove the residents, then re-skirt or screen the perimeter properly, with the vulnerable sections backed by buried wire. We do that work as a system; patching the one hole the animal used last night just changes which hole it uses tonight.

Roof rats in the urban canopy

Largo's roof rats are a canopy population — palms, laurel oaks, and citrus in the older neighbourhoods, connected by fences and utility lines into a road system above the streets. Rat work here combines trapping with the roofline audit: every vent, pipe penetration, and soffit gap closed in metal, and the palm and branch bridges to the roof identified so they can be cut back. Our work runs under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with your authorization as property owner; Florida has no nuisance-trapper license, whatever a competitor's website says. Native animals are relocated only on the rule's strict same-county terms, and nonnatives never — so the seal, as always, is the permanent part of the job.

Density changes the advice

On a dense Largo block we will sometimes tell you to coordinate with a neighbour — not because our work needs their permission, but because two sealed houses in a row change a raccoon's whole calculation, and your sealing dollars go further when the house on the route's other end is closed too. It is the kind of advice that only makes sense in a city built like this one, and it is free.

We quote it as a barn program, separate from any house sealing, after walking both.

faqs.q: I found a big snake in my Dunedin yard — what kind is it likely to be?
faqs.a: Most Florida snakes are nonvenomous and beneficial, and identification comes first. The venomous snakes in most of Florida are the cottonmouth, eastern diamondback rattlesnake, dusky pygmy rattlesnake, and harlequin coralsnake. A large, docile black snake may be an eastern indigo snake, which is federally Threatened — leave it alone, photograph it from a distance, and call FWC. Never handle a snake you cannot identify, and call us for an identification before anyone tries to move it.

faqs.q: Roof rats are in our downtown Dunedin attic. The palms touch the roof — is that the route?
faqs.a: Almost certainly one of them. Roof rats live in the palm canopy and travel frond to roof without touching the ground; on the downtown streets they also use the oak canopy and the utility lines. We seal the roofline entries in metal, trap out the residents, and give you the specific list of palm fronds and branches bridging to your roof so a trim closes the road. All three parts matter — sealing without the trim leaves the road open, and the trim without sealing leaves the doors.

faqs.q: We may have bats behind the fascia of our older Dunedin home. When can they come out?
faqs.a: Florida's bat calendar is set by law: exclusions run August 15 through April 15, and during the maternity season, April 16 to August 14, blocking bats is illegal because the young cannot fly. What we do in any season is confirm the colony, find every entry — free-tails use gaps as small as a fascia joint — and stage the job. If the report comes in spring, the exclusion is scheduled for the window's opening with every gap mapped; if a single bat is inside the living space, call the same day and we will advise on the spot.

Dunedin is the Pinellas city that kept its downtown, and its wildlife work starts there. The historic Main Street core and the neighbourhoods around it hold early-1900s homes and old commercial roofs a short walk from St. Joseph Sound — roof rats in the palms along the waterfront streets, raccoons in the tall old attics, and bats behind the fascia of buildings that have stood since the citrus trains ran. The Pinellas Trail cuts through town under a tunnel of oak canopy, and like every green corridor in this county, it is also an animal corridor: what lives along the trail lives, eventually, in the streets beside it.

Out from the core, Dunedin's waterfront does the talking. The causeway to Honeymoon Island, the marina district, and the canal and bayou streets put homes against open water and marsh grass, where raccoons work the seawalls and docks, opossums den under the waterfront decks, and the palms overhanging the roofs carry the rats. Dunedin's Scottish heritage gives it bagpipes and a highland games; its position on the Sound gives it the standard coastal-Florida animal list, delivered nightly along the water.
Dunedin.extendedBody:
Historic downtown roofs and the trail canopy

Dunedin's older homes reward a careful inspection. Roofs have been layered and joined across a century; the junctions where a porch roof or an addition meets the original house are where squirrels and roof rats get in, and the big oaks and palms overhanging the downtown streets provide the bridge. We seal those junctions in metal, cap the chimneys, and map the palm-to-roof contacts for your tree crew, because a rat exclusion that leaves the frond bridge standing is a job with an expiry date. On the historic commercial roofs along Main Street, the work is the same at larger scale — pigeons in the sign structures and rats in the roof voids are building problems, and they end with sealing, not scare devices.

The waterfront: seawalls, docks, and decks

Along the Sound and the bayous, raccoons commute the seawall line and den under waterfront decks and in boat houses; opossums and skunks take the same voids from the land side. Our waterfront inspections include the deck and dock structures, because sealing a Dunedin house while its deck void stays open to the seawall is solving the land half of a water problem. All of our work is done under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — and the sealing is always the permanent half of the job.

Bats and the August window

Brazilian free-tailed bats colonise the fascia gaps and roof voids of Dunedin's older buildings, often for years before the staining and smell give them away. Florida law fixes the calendar: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and blocking bats during the April 16 to August 14 maternity season is illegal. A colony reported in spring gets mapped and scheduled, then excluded completely when the window opens — one-way devices at the active entries, every secondary gap sealed — because a free-tailed colony that loses half its entries simply moves to the other half.

faqs.q: Raccoons own our Tarpon Springs dock area — what changes that?
faqs.a: The waste stream. Dock raccoons are professionals sustained by fish scraps, sponge-dock dumpsters, and pet food on porches; trapping thins them for a week. Locking dumpster lids, hosing cleaning stations into contained drains, and feeding no animal outdoors rewrites the dock's economics, and then trapping removes the residents who remain. We build both halves — the discipline changes with the business or homeowner, the trapping and dock-den exclusion with us — and the bayou goes back to herons.

faqs.q: Why is Safety Harbor squirrel work different from other towns?
faqs.a: The canopy never breaks. Philippe Park's oaks connect to the neighborhood oaks, which connect to your roof — a gray squirrel can commute the whole town at canopy height, so individual trapping without complete, metal-backed sealing simply rotates the population through your attic. Safety Harbor jobs are therefore seal-first in philosophy: trap the current tenants, close every corner and vent with materials that survive chewing, and trim the bridges. In this canopy, the seal is the service; the trap is the footnote.
